newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan opposition steps up pressure on Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition steps up pressure on Taleban.

text.p: Afghan opposition forces piled pressure on the Taleban as they moved to within 25 miles (40 km) of Kabul on Wednesday and were reported within range of one of the capital's main supply routes.
Opposition forces also reported repulsing a Taleban attack in the north of Afghanistan.

Taleban militia were pushed back about 12 miles (20 km) south, to positions between the towns of Qarabagh and Qaloqan, in heavy fighting that continued into Wednesday morning, residents fleeing the area said.
"The front line is now between Qarabagh and Qaloqan, and there was heavy fighting this morning, but it has quietened down," said one man who did not want to give his name.
He said he had driven his last remaining livestock -- a cow and its calf -- to Kabul to escape the fighting.

Since an unsuccessful attempt to capture the opposition stronghold in the north in May, the Taleban have suffered a number of defeats and significant losses of men and equipment, most recently in a number of abortive attacks on positions north of Kabul.

The opposition forces now north of Kabul are fighters loyal to Ahmed Shah Masood, the top military commander of the government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani ousted from Kabul by the purist Islamic Taleban last September.
Masood used his bases in the Panjsher valley -- close to the current front-line -- for almost 13 years to launch attacks against the communist government that was overthrown in 1992.

Eyewitnesses said on Wednesday that Taleban forces at a checkpoint on Khair Khana pass, on the northwestern outskirts of Kabul, were preventing people from moving down the road towards the front-line.
They were beating distraught villagers desperate to return to their families on the other side of the pass, the eyewitnesses said.
An opposition plane dropped a cluster bomb near the pass in mid-morning on Wednesday, wounding five people.
The bomb landed in an encampment of nomadic herders, whose usual migration route to the mountains in the north of the country has been blocked by the fighting.
"It was a miracle that there were not more dead and wounded," said an aid worker who witnessed the attack.
Opposition forces appeared to be preparing to open a new front-line to the east of Kabul.
A traveller who reached Kabul said anti-Taleban fighters had moved into range of Kabul's main supply route -- the road running east from Kabul to the Pakistan border at Torkham.

The traveller, who requested anonymity, said Masood forces were on high ground overlooking the town of Sarobi, 37 miles (60 km) east of Kabul, but added that there was no fighting in the area when he passed through.
Opposition forces said they had beaten back a Taleban offensive on the town of Taloqan, some 155 miles (250 km) north of Kabul, but the Taleban disputed this.

"They (the Taleban) attacked from their positions near Kunduz. We allowed them to come before counter-attacking and driving them back, they lost many men dead and captured," opposition spokesman Dr Abdullah (ed: one name) said on Wednesday morning.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), quoting Taleban spokesman Wakil Ahmed, reported that Taleban militia had captured Taloqan on Wednesday.
AIP said the Taleban shot down a helicopter as it was being flown out of the airport and captured a second chopper.
An aid worker based in Taloqan confirmed there had been fighting early on Wednesday morning, but said that by midday the town was calm.
